Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' appears trauma-incongruent unless there is a clear secondary road-traffic component; nothing elsewhere in the profile supports a vehicle-related trauma theme, so this trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the assault-focused profile.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is largely centered on interpersonal/ambient danger after assault (silence, unexpected sounds), but 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' suggests a broader environmental danger pattern. This is not inherently implausible, but combined with the car-crash trigger it contributes to a mismatched threat context that is not otherwise represented in memory or appraisals.

vignette: When Dr. Maya Patel was 51 and had earned her residency in internal medicine, the night she was walking to her office after a late-night shift the first time a white-haired man in a battered blue jacket cornered her on a dimly lit sidewalk. He thrust a knife into her chest, and the only sound was his ragged breathing and the hiss of a city siren as police arrived moments later. In the chaos, she clutched the exposed parts of her own body-the bruised forearm, the raw cut on her thigh-as if they might become the new targets of a future threat. That visceral image of her body parts, the authority presence of the police, and the very sight of the offender's silhouette became the anchors of her triggers, and from the first days after the assault she could not shake the idea that they would surface again at any moment. The assault shattered Maya's long-held beliefs that the world was safe and that her professional role as a doctor could protect her. She began to avoid any thought that might remind her of the event, convinced that if she allowed herself to think about it she would lose control. That thought avoidance hardened into a pervasive sense of threat-she felt danger lurking in any quiet room, in any sudden noise, in any stranger who approached her. Each time she was confronted by a sudden, unexpected sound or a sudden, empty silence, her mind immediately replayed the assault, and the terror she felt at that moment was almost identical to the terror she remembered from the night of the attack. The memories were vivid and frightening, even though they sometimes came with a sharp smell of burnt plastic and the metallic tang of blood-olfactory cues that only made the recall even more intense. Because her belief that the world was trustworthy had been ruined, even her memories of the assault felt unreal, as if they had been staged and she were merely an observer. In an effort to regain a sense of control, Maya started to gamble on online poker and bingo, hoping the rush of possibility would drown out the constant hum of fear. She also began wearing loose, concealing clothing in public, especially when she sensed a threat or when she saw the silhouette of a man in a similar jacket. She avoided any environment that might resemble the scene of the assault: she stopped walking the same shortcut she had taken before, and she refused to leave the hospital at night unless she was accompanied. These maladaptive strategies, driven by her negative appraisals, fed back into her sense of threat. The excitement of gambling amplified her feeling that danger was near; the concealing clothes made her feel both protected and paranoid, as if a threat could lurk behind any unfamiliar face. When she tried to confront a trigger-such as seeing a stranger in a white coat-she would feel a surge of anxiety that made her thoughts flash back to the knife and the police siren, reinforcing the terror she carried into everyday life. Over months Maya's avoidance became entrenched. In the hospital, she would pause at the nursing station to check her phone for a notification, hoping the distraction would soothe her. Yet every beep, every quiet pause between patient visits, intensified her sense of threat, causing her to avoid interactions, to keep her face hidden behind a stethoscope, and to retreat into a hypervigilant state. The more she avoided, the more she believed the world had betrayed her; each belief further fueled the threat she felt in silence and in loud sounds, which in turn led her to gamble more, to conceal more, and to hide from triggers that were now part of her everyday reality. In this closed loop, her memory of the assault-still vivid with smell and terror-was both the spark that ignited her threat and the fire that fed her negative beliefs, which then fed her avoidance and maladaptive coping, closing the cycle of distress. It was a particularly stressful morning at the hospital, when a new resident approached her with a difficult case and asked a question that reminded Maya of the moment the offender's knife slid across her ribs. She felt her heart pound, her breath shallow, and an overwhelming sense of dread sweep through her. She realized she could no longer function in the same way she had before. The night she finally called a therapist was after she had refused to see a patient because the sound of a stethoscope's beep made her feel as if she were hearing the same echo as the assault. Maya was most afraid that her world would never feel safe again, but she was also hopeful that with help she could untangle the loop that had made every night, every quiet pause, and every encounter with strangers a threat to her well-being.
